title: The Silver Line
subtitle: Argent, Colorado, Monday 22 to Tuesday 30 September 1879

listing.title: The Silver Line 🚂
listing.blurb: Colorado, 1879: two railroads racing for a silver camp at ten thousand feet, one with lawyers and debts, one with gunmen and gold. You are hired to guard the first silver train out of Argent on Saturday. Somebody on that train means to rob it, the pass is being sabotaged, the track gangs are on strike, and the man who planned it all is shaking your hand. Levels 3–7.

synopsis: Argent is a silver camp of four thousand people in a high basin of the Sawatch Range, two years old, ten thousand six hundred feet up, and rich enough to have two newspapers, a brass band, a smelter and a waiting list for coffins. In September 1879 it has no railroad, and two are racing to reach it. The Denver, Argent and Pacific, a narrow-gauge line out of Denver, is laying its last miles down from Hollowell Pass, run in the field by a brilliant, sleepless chief engineer, Winfield Coburn, on borrowed money, Boston bonds and company scrip. The Great Plains and Pacific, a standard-gauge line out of Kansas, is coming up from the south with gold coin, better wages, a construction boss named Roy Brannock who builds stone forts on disputed grades, and a county sheriff in its pocket. Whichever railroad wins the Argent Compact wins five years of the basin's ore and bullion: the Mining Association has promised its freight to the first line that carries a shipment of at least $75,000 in Argent bullion by rail from the Argent depot to a Denver main-line connection, whole, before midnight on Tuesday 30 September. The DA&P means to do it on Saturday 27 September with the first through train: one hundred and thirty bars of silver, $180,000 declared, from Hester Ruane's Argent Reduction Works and from the Lodestar, the famous mine of Aurelius Stannard, the camp's founder, first citizen and president of the Mining Association. The party is hired to guard that train. In the six days before it runs, the camp's assayer dies in a locked office, a rockslide kills two Chinese graders at Hollowell Cut, a trestle burns, the DA&P's track gangs strike over scrip, a mob forms, and a known train robber is seen at the faro table. Some of this is the Great Plains and Pacific playing rough. The robbery is something else. It is being planned from inside, by a man who needs the silver train to be robbed more than anyone needs it to arrive, and Saturday's run over Hollowell Pass, with its trestle, its four-percent grade and its forgotten spur, is the most exciting two hours anyone in Argent will ever spend.
hook: Argent, Colorado, Monday 22 September 1879, eleven in the morning, in the ore yard of the Argent Reduction Works. The smelter stacks are pouring yellow smoke into a sky so blue it hurts, the stamp mills up the gulch are going like a thousand blacksmiths, and somewhere down the valley a steam whistle answers: the DA&P's work train, three miles out and coming. Hester Ruane, who owns the smelter and is the only woman on the Argent Mining Association, has asked each of you here for a different reason, and you are looking at each other across a stack of silver bars the length of a coffin. She is a square, grey, sunburned widow of fifty in a man's coat, and she does not waste words. On Saturday, she says, the first train leaves Argent with a hundred and thirty bars of silver, and if it reaches Hollowell Junction whole, this camp has a railroad and her smelter lives. The Continental Express Company has had a tip that someone means to rob it. The county sheriff does not answer letters. She will pay each of you $200 to see the silver over the pass, and $1,000 more among you when it is signed for at the Junction. Then she says the part she has not told the Association: a known train robber's right-hand man was at the faro table at the Silver Dollar last night, and her friend the assayer, who weighed every bar in this yard, was found dead yesterday morning, and she does not believe it was an accident. Down the valley, the whistle blows again.

setting.name: Argent and Hollowell Pass, Sawatch Range, Colorado, 22 to 30 September 1879
setting.description: Argent is fictional; the year, the state and the silver boom are real. Colorado has been a state for three years, Leadville over the next range is the richest silver camp in the world, and two real railroads are fighting over the Arkansas canyon with lawyers and rifles, which everyone in Argent reads about in the Denver papers. Argent sits in a bowl of bare red and grey peaks at ten thousand six hundred feet, a single long street of false fronts and log cabins laid out along Argent Creek, with the mines up the gulches on every side: the Lodestar, the biggest, high on Lodestar Hill above town with its mill and its tramway; a dozen smaller mines and two hundred claims; and at the lower end of town, by the new depot, the smoke of Hester Ruane's Argent Reduction Works, the only smelter in the basin. The railroads come in from the east. The DA&P has built up Hollowell Canyon from its junction with the Denver main line, thirty-one miles away, through a narrow defile called the Narrows, over Hollowell Pass at eleven thousand five hundred feet, and down the west side across the Needle Creek trestle, through the grading camp at Hollowell Cut, past the old Blind Tom spur, to a railhead two miles above town; its last spike is set for Friday. The GP&P is coming up the south fork from the Arkansas valley to its railhead camp at Burnt Mule Flats, nine miles from Argent, and claims in court that the Narrows was its survey first. The people are everyone the boom has pulled in: Cornish miners on Cornish Row with their Bible Christian chapel; Irish tracklayers; Welsh and German and Swedish muckers; Hispano and Mexican tie-cutters, packers and graders from the San Luis Valley and northern New Mexico; a Chinese grading company of sixty-one men at the Cut, barred from the basin itself by a Miners' Union resolution; Black cowhands, soldiers and cooks; Kansas farm boys and Exodusters from Nicodemus on the GP&P's crews; card dealers, laundresses, lawyers, a lady doctor and a newspaper editor who sleeps under her press.
setting.atmosphere: Thin air: everyone is short of breath for a week, whisky hits twice as hard, water boils before it is hot and coffee is never strong enough. The light is enormous and the sky is dark blue at noon; there was frost in the ruts this morning and there will be snow on the pass by October. The stamp mills never stop, day or night, and newcomers cannot sleep for a week and then cannot sleep without them. The smelter smoke is sulphur-yellow and smells of rotten eggs and money. Mud, mules, ore wagons, a brass band practising for Saturday. The Silver Dollar's piano, the Methodist hymns on Cornish Row, a Spanish song at the packers' corral, a Cantonese work song carrying down from the Cut. Gunfire on Saturday night, mostly at the sky. The tone is a western paperback: hard men, hard women, a long fall from a trestle, a gunfight in the snow, a train going like the wind and a man who will not back down. Violence is quick and has consequences; most problems can be talked, bought, outfaced or outthought before they are shot.

regions.name: Argent
regions.description: The camp. Front Street, a quarter mile of false fronts on Argent Creek: the Silver Dollar saloon and gambling hall, the Clarion office, the Grand Central Hotel, Wertheimer's dry goods, the Continental Express office, three churches, eleven saloons and Llew Treharne's log calaboose. Assay Street, where Erasmus Ashworth's assay office stands shuttered. Cornish Row up the hill, the miners' cabins and the chapel. The new DA&P depot at the lower end of town, its paint still wet, beside the Argent Reduction Works and its ore yard. Above it all on Lodestar Hill, the Lodestar mine, its mill, and Aurelius Stannard's white house with the only lawn in the basin.

regions.name: The West Slope of the Pass
regions.description: The DA&P's last miles, from the railhead two miles above Argent up to the summit. The Blind Tom spur at mile three, an old construction siding that runs half a mile into Blind Tom Gulch to the abandoned Blind Tom mine and its ore platform. Hollowell Cut at mile four, the grading camp: the Irish tracklayers' tents and Bridget Cahill's boarding tent, the Hispano graders' camp, and at the upper end, Ong Pak-wai's company. The DA&P powder house above the Cut. The Needle Creek trestle at mile five, three hundred and eighty feet long and ninety feet high over a white-water creek, the most photographed thing in the county. The Horseshoe, a curve blasted into the cliff beyond it, and the four-percent climb to the summit at mile seven.

regions.name: Hollowell Canyon and the Narrows
regions.description: The east side: twenty-four miles of DA&P track down from the summit through Hollowell Canyon, a gorge so tight in its lower reach, the Narrows, that there is room for one railroad and the river and nothing else. Both railroads claim the Narrows. The GP&P has filed in a Kansas-friendly court, and Roy Brannock has built two stone forts on the canyon rim above it, which he calls survey stations. At the bottom, Hollowell Junction: a water tank, a telegraph office, a Continental Express transfer shed and the DA&P main line to Denver.

regions.name: Burnt Mule Flats
regions.description: The Great Plains and Pacific's railhead camp on the south fork, nine miles from Argent by wagon road: a standard-gauge yard, a commissary, a saloon in a tent, eight hundred workers paid in gold coin every Saturday, and Roy Brannock's private car, the Wichita, on a siding with armed guards. From here the GP&P is grading a line toward Argent over Burnt Mule Pass, which it cannot finish before the snow. Its men are Irish, Swedish, Black and white Kansans and Exodusters, and they are not all Brannock's.

campaignRules.name: The Compact Clock
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on a fixed nine-day calendar, Monday 22 to Tuesday 30 September 1879, and the opposition acts on it whether or not the players are watching. sl-scenario-001 is Monday and Tuesday (the camp and the hiring), sl-scenario-002 is Wednesday to Friday (sabotage in the pass, the strike, the last spike), sl-scenario-003 is Saturday morning (the train), sl-scenario-004 is Saturday afternoon to Tuesday midnight (the aftermath and the grade). The unit of time is the scene, about two hours; a day has six to eight. The Argent Compact deadline is midnight on Tuesday 30 September: the first railroad to carry at least $75,000 of Argent bullion by rail from the Argent depot to a Denver main-line connection, whole, wins. Tell the players the date and time at the start of every scene, and what the railroads, the strikers and the gang did with the scenes the players spent elsewhere.

campaignRules.name: Reputation in Argent
campaignRules.description: The party shares one Reputation score for Argent and the pass, from −5 to +5, tracked openly by the GM and announced when it changes (frontier.json, reputation). It starts at 0: strangers with guns, hired by the smelter widow. It rises by 1 for keeping your word in public, standing up to a bully, paying a debt, protecting a worker of any background, or bringing in a prisoner alive; by 2 for stopping a lynching or saving the train. It falls by 1 for bullying, cheating at cards and being caught, taking a bribe that becomes known, or backing down from a fair challenge; by 2 for shooting an unarmed man or taking a side in the strike with a gun. At +3 the Silver Dollar extends credit, the Clarion prints your side, and miners join a posse on your word. At −3 the stores close to you and Sheriff Riggs finds a warrant. The workers' camps at the Cut keep their own count, which the GM tracks privately and reveals when it matters.

campaignRules.name: Three Clues
campaignRules.description: Every conclusion the players must reach has at least three clues in different places, named in each scenario (sl-scenario files list them as A1, A2 and so on). A core clue is found automatically by anyone who looks in the right place with a relevant skill or the right question; rolls only add detail, speed or a bonus. A failed roll costs time, Reputation or a favour, never the case. If the players are stuck, a companion summarises what the party knows aloud, or a person with a reason to talk comes to them.

campaignRules.name: Every Hand Has a Name
campaignRules.description: The workers on both railroads, Irish, Chinese, Cornish, Hispano and Mexican, Black and white, Kansan and Swede, are people with names, families, wages owed and opinions, and the GM plays them that way: never as menace, background or comic relief. Their spokesmen (Bridget Cahill, Teodoro Gallegos, Ong Pak-wai, Hannibal Stokes) negotiate, testify, refuse and act on their own interests. Prejudice in the camp (the Miners' Union resolution against the Chinese, the mob at the Cut) is shown as what it is: a crime waiting to happen, which decent people stand against. No slurs, in narration or dialogue.

explorationRules: This is a camp-and-railroad campaign, and the map is a schematic of the west slope of Hollowell Pass and the canyon beyond: Argent at the western end, the DA&P line climbing east past the Blind Tom spur, Hollowell Cut and the Needle Creek trestle to the summit, then down Hollowell Canyon through the Narrows to the Junction; the GP&P's railhead at Burnt Mule Flats to the south. Distances are real: Argent to the Cut is four miles (an hour on horseback, two on foot, twenty minutes by work train when one is running), Argent to Burnt Mule Flats nine miles by wagon road (two hours riding), the summit to the Junction twenty-four miles of canyon. Use frontier.json for trail travel, horses and weather: the pass is at eleven thousand five hundred feet, nights are below freezing, and a storm on Thursday leaves snow on the summit. Within Argent the unit of time is the scene; on the trail it is the hour. Investigation follows the three-clue rule: core clues are automatic for anyone who looks in the right place with the right skill; rolls add detail or speed, and failure costs time or Reputation, never the case. Showdowns use frontier.json: let a stare-down end one, and remember a fair fight and an unfair one look very different to the camp. Between scenes let the camp breathe: the stamp mills, the smelter whistle at six, the brass band practising, a packer singing to his mules, a funeral on Cornish Row, a Cantonese work song from the Cut, the work train's whistle getting closer every day. The players should come away feeling they rode that train.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only; it does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Argent, Hollowell Pass, both railroads, the Continental Express Company and every person in this campaign are fictional. The year, Colorado, the silver boom, Leadville, the narrow-gauge and standard-gauge railroad wars of 1879, company scrip, the Miners' Union resolutions against Chinese workers in Colorado camps, the Central Pacific's Chinese crews, the Exodusters, the 10th Cavalry and the federal laws on the mails and railroad rights-of-way are real. No real person appears.
controlFile.theTruth: Aurelius Stannard, 58, the founder of Argent, the president of its Mining Association and the owner of the Lodestar, is ruined and nobody knows it. The Lodestar's main vein pinched out in January 1879. Since then Stannard has kept the mine's reputation alive by buying ore from small claims at twice the market price through his mill foreman Obed Becket, by paying dividends in cash out of the last of his capital, and by having his own mill cast bullion bars that are silver jackets over lead cores, stamped with the Lodestar's mark and a false fineness. On the strength of the Lodestar's name he has floated Lodestar Consolidated in New York, offering $500,000 of stock to the public; subscriptions close on Wednesday 1 October. Saturday's train carries seventy Lodestar bars declared at $96,000 and guaranteed at that value by the Continental Express Company, alongside sixty honest bars from Hester Ruane's smelter worth $84,000. If the Lodestar bars reach the Denver mint, the first assay exposes him and the New York offering collapses. If they are robbed, nobody ever assays them, Continental pays him $96,000, and the most famous train robbery in Colorado makes the Lodestar's name. So Stannard has arranged to have his own silver stolen. Through Becket he hired Rafe Gorham, a cool, clever horse thief and train robber out of Missouri and the Nevada State Prison, and promised him the whole express car: the Lodestar bars, which Gorham believes are the richest, and Ruane's, which are real. The plan, Stannard's own: he asked Coburn, as a security measure, to put the express car at the rear of the train, ahead of the caboose, so that robbers who stop the engine would have to go through the passengers. Gorham bought the DA&P rear brakeman, Tobe Kersey, by paying his $340 faro debt. On Saturday, beyond the Needle Creek trestle, Gorham's lieutenant Asa Varley and six riders stop the train with a felled pine at the Horseshoe curve and pin it down with rifle fire; in the caboose, Kersey pulls the coupling pin ahead of the express car and releases the brakes, and two of Gorham's men, the Haney brothers, riding on passes Stannard signed as Lodestar shift bosses, take the express car while it rolls back down the grade. A charge of stolen DA&P dynamite on the trestle is fired behind it so the engine cannot follow. Gorham's man Sully Mapes has thrown and padlocked the Blind Tom switch after the train passed, so the runaway car runs into the spur and coasts to a stop at the abandoned ore platform, where Gorham, four men and three wagons wait, with Becket, who is there to see the Lodestar bars go and to kill Kersey as a loose end. Separately: Stannard also has a hedge. If the DA&P fails the Compact, the Association chooses again and Stannard has the casting vote, which he has sold to Roy Brannock of the GP&P for $20,000 in GP&P stock, by letter. Brannock knows nothing of the robbery; his own sabotage of the pass (the rockslide at the Cut, the trestle fire, the agitator in the strike) is a separate and cruder campaign to make the DA&P miss the deadline. On Saturday 20 September the assayer Erasmus Ashworth, who had been asked to stamp the Lodestar bars without drilling them and had secretly drilled one, told Becket he was going to Mrs. Ruane on Monday. Becket, on Stannard's instruction to see that Erasmus kept quiet until the train had gone, came to the assay office at eleven that night, struck him behind the ear with a sap, laid him by the furnace, and wired the flue damper shut from the roof. The coroner, who is also the undertaker and is paid by the Lodestar to bury its dead, called it an accident on Sunday. One more thing binds the case to the race: the Association certifies the Compact shipment, Stannard chairs it, and he can rule a shipment that arrives without the Lodestar bars 'not whole'. If he is exposed or in custody, the vice president, Hester Ruane, presides instead.
suspects: Aurelius Stannard, 58, Lodestar Hill: the camp's founder and the Mining Association's president. Motive: the Lodestar is played out, its bars are lead, and his New York offering closes on 1 October. Plan: have the train robbed of his own bars, collect $96,000 from Continental, never be assayed. He ordered Erasmus Ashworth silenced. THIS IS THE INSIDE JOB, AND IT SUCCEEDS IF NOBODY INTERFERES.

Roy Brannock, 46, Burnt Mule Flats: construction boss of the Great Plains and Pacific. Motive: the Compact; if the DA&P misses midnight Tuesday, the GP&P can buy the Association's vote and, in the courts, the Narrows. Plan: sabotage (the rockslide, the trestle fire, an agitator in the strike) through his agent Virgil Tench, and on Saturday, seizing the Narrows with armed men while everyone watches the train. Guilty of the sabotage and of the deaths of Leung Ah-sing and Chan Yiu; innocent of the robbery, and furious when he learns of it.

Winfield Coburn, 39, the DA&P's chief engineer and field boss. Motive for suspicion: the DA&P is bankrupt in all but name, it pays in scrip, and the Continental guarantee would pay out on a robbery. In truth he would rather die than lose the Compact; he is the race's most sympathetic obsessive, and he put the express car at the rear because Stannard asked him to.

Hester Ruane, 50, the Argent Reduction Works: the party's employer. Motive for suspicion: her bars are guaranteed too. In truth her smelter dies without a railroad and she wants the train to arrive more than anyone alive.

Rafe Gorham, 41, gang leader, out of Missouri and the Nevada State Prison. The robber, not the plotter: he believes the Lodestar bars are the prize. When he finds lead under the silver he will come for Stannard, and he is the best witness against him.
Obed Becket, 35, the Lodestar mill foreman: Stannard's go-between and the man who killed Erasmus Ashworth.
Tobe Kersey, 24, DA&P rear brakeman: bought for $340; frightened, and marked by Becket for death at the Blind Tom platform.
redHerrings: Roy Brannock looks exactly like the man who would rob the train: he gains most from its failure, his agent Tench is in the camp stirring the strike, his men burned the trestle. The players should believe it through sl-scenario-002. He is a saboteur, a bully and responsible for two deaths, but the robbery is not his, and his letter buying Stannard's vote (found in sl-scenario-004) makes him look more guilty while actually pointing at Stannard.

Paddy Rooney, if played, is a convicted express-car robber who shared a prison with Gorham; NPCs (Sheriff Riggs, the Clarion's rival paper, Stannard himself) will suggest he is the inside man. He is not. If Paddy is not played, Coburn's new powder man, a stranger, plays the same role.

Ong Pak-wai's company is blamed for the rockslide and then for the trestle fire by Tench and the Miners' Union. The evidence clears them completely (E clues); the mob at the Cut on Thursday night is the campaign's moral test.

Merritt Strickland, the Continental Express messenger, is nervous, secretive and asks too many questions about the consist. He is the Continental Express Company's own detective, sent because of the tip, and he will reveal himself to Isaac Merriweather or anyone who shows him a badge (sl-scenario-001).
Hester Ruane's insurance and Coburn's scrip both look like motives for an inside job. Neither is.
clues: A. GIDEON ASHWORTH WAS MURDERED. A1: the bruise behind his left ear, under the hair (the body, at the undertaker's; Phoebe Lanyon's notebook) (sl-scenario-001). A2: fresh copper wire twisted round the flue damper from the outside, on the roof (the assay office) (sl-scenario-001). A3: the assay ledger's pages for 13 to 20 September are cut out with a razor (the assay office) (sl-scenario-001). A4: Llew Treharne saw Obed Becket on Assay Street at 11:30 on Saturday night (sl-scenario-001 or later). A5: Gertrud Haas, whose boarding house shares a wall with the office, heard a knock after eleven and Erasmus say 'Obed, it is late' (sl-scenario-001).

B. THE LODESTAR IS PLAYED OUT AND ITS BARS ARE NOT WHAT THEY SAY. B1: Erasmus's private duplicate assay book, in the drawer of his chess box (left to Phoebe in his will): Lodestar ore down from 310 ounces a ton to under 6 since January (sl-scenario-001). B2: in the same box, an envelope marked 'L. bar 41, plug': a drill core of silver skin over grey lead (sl-scenario-001). B3: Lydia Marchmont's share: every dividend paid in new Denver banknotes, never bullion, and the books refused to a part-owner (sl-scenario-001). B4: the Lodestar Consolidated prospectus in the New York papers at the Clarion office, promising reserves of $4 million (sl-scenario-001 or 002). B5: Cap'n Hender Rosevear, the Lodestar's mine captain, through Mercy Pengelly: 'there's nowt left in her since January' (sl-scenario-001 or 002). B6: small claim-owners sold ore to the Lodestar mill at twice the market price through Becket (sl-scenario-001 or 002).

C. SOMEONE MEANS TO ROB THE SATURDAY TRAIN FROM INSIDE. C1: Asa Varley, Gorham's lieutenant, at the Silver Dollar faro table, recognised by Paddy Rooney or from the Continental circular (sl-scenario-001). C2: the Continental Express tip, and the messenger Strickland's real job (sl-scenario-001). C3: Tobe Kersey paid a $340 faro debt at the Silver Dollar on Monday night in new gold eagles (sl-scenario-001). C4: the consist: the express car is to run at the rear, 'at the Association's request' (Coburn's order book, Strickland's complaint) (sl-scenario-001 or 003). C5: on Tuesday night the DA&P powder house is opened with a key and forty sticks of dynamite and fifty caps are gone (sl-scenario-001 end, examined in 002).

D. THE GP&P (BRANNOCK, THROUGH TENCH) SABOTAGED THE PASS. D1: Vulcan Powder Works wrappers, a GP&P brand, and fresh drill holes on the ledge above the rockslide (sl-scenario-002). D2: coal-oil cans stencilled GP&P COMMISSARY in Needle Creek below the burned trestle (sl-scenario-002). D3: the teamster Lem Hadley, drunk and frightened, paid $50 in gold by Tench to drive a wagon to the trestle (sl-scenario-002). D4: Tench's horse, branded with the GP&P's Circle K, tracked from the trestle to Burnt Mule Flats (sl-scenario-002).

E. ONG PAK-WAI'S COMPANY DID NOT CAUSE THE SLIDE AND IS BEING FRAMED. E1: the slide was blasted from a ledge sixty feet above the cut where Ong's daybook shows no man worked, and the drill holes are fresh (sl-scenario-002). E2: the wrappers are Vulcan, a GP&P brand; Ong's company draws DA&P powder by signed chit, and the chits balance (sl-scenario-002). E3: Leung Ah-sing and Chan Yiu died asleep in their tent at 4 a.m., when no blasting is ever done (Phoebe, or the camp's own record) (sl-scenario-002). E4: Tench bought the whiskey for Thursday's Miners' Union meeting and told it the Chinese burned the trestle (sl-scenario-002).

F. THE STRIKE IS REAL, AND TENCH WANTS IT TO BECOME A RIOT. F1: DA&P scrip is redeemable only at the company store at a 20 percent discount, and is three weeks behind (sl-scenario-002). F2: Ong's daybook and Bridget Cahill's committee both show $11,600 owed to the crews (sl-scenario-002). F3: Tench was in Bridget's tent on Tuesday offering GP&P jobs at gold wages to any man who walked off (sl-scenario-002). F4: Stannard offers Coburn a $12,000 cash loan to pay the crews in coin, on condition the train runs Saturday, which is generous and strange (sl-scenario-002; also points to H).

G. THE STOLEN DA&P DYNAMITE AND THE BLIND TOM SPUR ARE FOR THE TRAIN. G1: the powder house padlock was opened with a DA&P key; rear brakemen carry one (sl-scenario-002). G1b: Pablo Quintana rented three mules to Tobe Kersey on Tuesday for $15 in gold (sl-scenario-002). G2: none of the sabotage used DA&P powder (D1, E2), so the forty sticks are still somewhere (sl-scenario-002). G3: Ong's foreman Yee Kam-ling saw three riders lead loaded mules up Blind Tom Gulch at nine on Tuesday night (sl-scenario-002). G4: at the Blind Tom ore platform, a cache of dynamite, a tent, fresh wagon tracks, and the switch padlock replaced with a new one (sl-scenario-002). G5: on Friday night, sticks wired to two bents of the rebuilt trestle (sl-scenario-002 end or 003).

H. STANNARD IS BEHIND THE ROBBERY. H1: a bullet, an axe or a curious knife exposes grey lead under the skin of a Lodestar bar (sl-scenario-003). H2: the Haney brothers ride in the caboose on passes signed by Stannard as Lodestar shift bosses (sl-scenario-003). H3: Coburn: putting the express car at the rear was Stannard's suggestion (sl-scenario-001, 002 or 003). H4: Becket at the Blind Tom platform with Gorham (sl-scenario-003 or 004). H5: Gorham, once he has seen the lead, names Stannard and Becket (sl-scenario-004). H6: Stannard's Saturday telegram to his New York brokers, CLOSE SUBSCRIPTION EARLY STOP WIRE FUNDS, and the Continental guarantee for $96,000 (sl-scenario-004). H7: Stannard demands that the posse shoot Gorham on sight (sl-scenario-004).

I. BECKET KILLED ASHWORTH ON STANNARD'S ORDER. I1: a spool of the same copper wire and a leather sap in Becket's room at the Lodestar mill (sl-scenario-004). I2: Becket's boot nails match the scuffs on the assay office roof (sl-scenario-001 noted, matched in 004). I3: Kersey, if saved from Becket, heard Becket brag of 'the assayer' (sl-scenario-003 or 004). I4: Becket's own confession, given to save his neck (sl-scenario-004).
controlFile.theInsideJob: The players crack the campaign when they understand that the Lodestar's silver is not real. Once they know that, everything lines up: Erasmus died because he drilled a bar, Stannard's cash dividends and his New York offering are a fraud, his eagerness to lend Coburn money so the train runs on Saturday is a man who needs a robbery, and the express car at the rear is his idea. Point the B clues hard in sl-scenario-001 and 002, and let the players suspect Brannock for the robbery as long as they like; the sabotage really is his. If the party reaches Saturday without suspecting the Lodestar, H1 (a bar shot open in the express car) is the moment, and Phoebe Lanyon or Mercy Pengelly should know lead when they see it. Stannard never fights. He is genial, generous and helpful until he is cornered, and then he tries to buy, then to flee, then to have someone else shoot.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no single right ending, only consequences. THE TRAIN: if nobody interferes, the express car is stolen at the Blind Tom platform, Kersey is shot by Becket, the trestle is blown and the DA&P misses the Compact. If the party saves the car, or recovers the real silver and gets sixty Ruane bars ($84,000, enough on its own) to Hollowell Junction by midnight Tuesday, the DA&P wins the Compact and Argent has its railroad. THE NARROWS: Brannock's men hold the canyon from Saturday afternoon; the train can get through by the federal mail (Isaac Merriweather's star: obstructing the United States mail is a federal crime), by a federal injunction from Denver carried by telegraph and courier, by Ong's back route for the silver on Pablo's mules, by persuading the GP&P's own workers not to fight for the men who killed Leung Ah-sing and Chan Yiu, or by force, which costs lives on both sides. STANNARD: he is untouchable on rumour; he falls on evidence: the lead bars, Erasmus's book, Gorham's or Becket's testimony, the telegram. Then Llew Treharne arrests him, Lodestar Consolidated collapses before it takes a dollar of public money, and Continental pays nothing. If he is not exposed, he collects $96,000 and leaves for New York, and the miners of Argent are paid in Lodestar paper all winter. GORHAM: he wants Stannard dead and his own silver; he can be taken, bargained with, or faced in a showdown on Front Street on Monday at sundown. THE WORKERS: whether the crews are paid in coin, whether Ong's company is cleared and paid and its dead sent home, whether the mob at the Cut is stopped, are the consequences the camp remembers longest. Argent gets a railroad either way, in time: it is 1879. The question the campaign asks is who pays for it.
